title: Byblis
titleEn: Byblis, and the Letter Begun — Metamorphoses IX.418–529
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The gods are still complaining that Iolaus and the sons of Callirhoe have been given their youth back, each god pressing the claim of a favourite, until Jupiter tells them that the Fates rule him as well: his own sons Aeacus, Rhadamanthus and Minos are growing old, and Minos is despised for it. From the aged Minos the poem turns to Miletus, who fled him, founded a city in Asia that bears his name, and fathered twins on Cyanee — Byblis and Caunus. Byblis falls in love with her brother, and this part follows the long soliloquy in which she argues with herself: first disowning the dream that showed her what she wants, then finding precedents for it among the gods, then renouncing it, then resolving to confess it in a letter. It closes with her at the wax tablets, writing, erasing and writing again, having just deleted the word “sister”.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi faticano venturi praescia dixit
ore Themis, vario superi sermone fremebant,
et “cur non aliis eadem dare dona liceret”
murmur erat:
sentences.l:
When Themis, foreknowing of what was about to come, had said these things
with her fate-singing mouth, the gods above were murmuring with talk of every kind,
and “why should it not be allowed to give the same gifts to others?” —
that was the murmuring:
sentences.i: When Themis had said all this with her fate-singing mouth, knowing what was to come, the gods above fell to murmuring, each with his own talk, and the grumble that went round was: why should the same gifts not be allowed to others?
sentences.n: faticano is a rare compound of fatum and cano, “fate-singing”, and Magnus keeps it here. praescia takes the genitive venturi, itself the future participle of venio used as a noun: “foreknowing of the thing about to come”. The grumble is quoted with liceret, imperfect subjunctive, because it reports the question the gods were putting: “why should it not be allowed?”

sentences.t:
queritur veteres Pallantias annos
coniugis esse sui, queritur canescere mitis
Iasiona Ceres, repetitum Mulciber aevum
poscit Erichthonio.
sentences.l:
Pallantias complains that the years of her own husband
are old ones; gentle Ceres complains that Iasion is turning grey;
Mulciber demands a lifetime fetched back again
for Erichthonius.
sentences.i: Aurora complains that her husband's years are old ones; gentle Ceres complains that Iasion is going grey; Vulcan demands that Erichthonius have his lifetime given back to him.
sentences.n: Pallantias is Aurora, daughter of Pallas, whose husband Tithonus was given immortality without youth. Both complaints run through an accusative and infinitive after queritur: veteres annos esse, canescere Iasiona. mitis is nominative singular and belongs to Ceres, held apart from its noun across the line-end — “gentle Ceres”; Iasion was her mortal lover. Mulciber is Vulcan, father of Erichthonius; Erichthonio is a dative of advantage, “for Erichthonius”.

sentences.t:
Venerem quoque cura futuri
tangit et Anchisae renovare paciscitur annos.
sentences.l:
Care for what is about to come touches Venus too,
and she bargains to renew the years of Anchises.
sentences.i: Venus too is touched by anxiety about the future, and strikes a bargain of her own: to give Anchises back his years.
sentences.n: futuri is the future participle used as a noun again, matching venturi at line 418 — “care for the thing to come”. paciscitur is deponent, passive in form and active in meaning: she is the one bargaining. Anchises was Venus' mortal lover, and mortal is exactly the trouble: every god in this list has loved someone who ages.

sentences.t:
Cui studeat, deus omnis habet, crescitque favore
turbida seditio, donec sua Iuppiter ora
solvit et “o nostri siqua est reverentia,” dixit
“quo ruitis?
sentences.l:
Every god has someone to take the side of, and the turbulent
revolt swells with partisanship, until Jupiter unsealed
his own lips and said, “O, if there is any reverence for me,
where are you rushing?
sentences.i: Every god has his own favourite, and the unruly mutiny swells as each takes a side, until Jupiter opened his mouth: “If there is any respect for me at all — where are you rushing?
sentences.n: cui studeat is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive: “someone for him to be eager about”; studeo takes the dative. seditio is a political word — mutiny, a faction rising — and Ovid keeps the gods' quarrel in the language of the forum. nostri is an objective genitive, “reverence directed at me”, with Jupiter using the plural of himself. sua ... ora is a poetic plural for one mouth.

sentences.t:
Tantumne aliquis sibi posse videtur,
fata quoque ut superet?
sentences.l:
Does anyone seem to himself to have so much power
that he may overcome even the fates?
sentences.i: Does anyone imagine he has power enough to beat the Fates as well?
sentences.n: The -ne attached to tantumne marks the question. tantum ... ut sets up a result clause with superet. quoque here is the plain adverb “also, even” — but the same spelling can be quo-que, “and by which”, so it is always worth a second look; you will meet the other kind shortly. sibi videtur is “seems to himself”, that is, imagines.

sentences.t:
Fatis Iolaus in annos,
quos egit, rediit, fatis iuvenescere debent
Callirhoe geniti, non ambitione nec armis.
sentences.l:
By the fates Iolaus went back into the years
which he had lived through; by the fates must the sons
begotten of Callirhoe grow young — not by lobbying, nor by arms.
sentences.i: It was by the Fates that Iolaus returned to the years he had already lived; it is by the Fates that Callirhoe's sons must grow young again — not by canvassing, and not by force.
sentences.n: fatis is an ablative of means, placed first in both halves and repeated: the point of the whole speech. Callirhoe is an ablative of origin without a preposition, “begotten from Callirhoe”. ambitio is the word for going round soliciting votes — Jupiter is calling the gods' pleading electioneering, and armis threatens what electioneering turns into.

sentences.t:
Vos etiam, quoque hoc animo meliore feratis,
me quoque fata regunt.
sentences.l:
You too — and, so that you may bear this with a better spirit,
me too — the fates govern.
sentences.i: The Fates rule you; and — so that you may take it the better — the Fates rule me as well.
sentences.n: Two different words spelled quoque stand a line apart here, and this is the clearest case of that trap in the tale. The first, quoque hoc animo meliore feratis, is quo + -que: quo introduces a purpose clause, as it regularly does when a comparative like meliore stands inside it — “and in order that you may bear this the better”. The second, me quoque, is the ordinary adverb “also”. The single verb regunt governs both vos etiam and me quoque, split apart by the parenthesis.

sentences.t:
Quae si mutare valerem,
nec nostrum seri curvarent Aeacon anni,
perpetuumque aevi florem Rhadamanthus haberet
cum Minoe meo, qui propter amara senectae
pondera despicitur nec quo prius ordine regnat.”
sentences.l:
And if I had the power to change these things,
late years would not be bending down our Aeacus,
and Rhadamanthus would keep the unfading flower of life
together with my Minos, who, because of the bitter
weights of old age, is looked down on and no longer reigns in the rank he held before.”
sentences.i: And if I had the power to change all that, the late years would not be stooping my own Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus would keep the flower of life unfading, and my Minos with him — Minos, who is despised now for the bitter weight of his old age, and no longer reigns with the standing he once had.”
sentences.n: quae opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and these things”, the decrees just named — not as a relative clause hanging on what precedes. The whole is a present contrary-to-fact condition: valerem, curvarent, haberet. Aeacon and, just below, Rhadamanthon and Minoa keep their Greek endings in the accusative. despicitur is passive: Minos is looked down on, not looking down. quo prius ordine is an ablative, “in the rank in which he reigned before”.

sentences.t:
Dicta Iovis movere deos, nec sustinet ullus,
cum videat fessos Rhadamanthon et Aeacon annis
et Minoa, queri.
sentences.l:
The words of Jupiter moved the gods, and not one holds out
to complain, when he sees Rhadamanthus and Aeacus worn out by their years,
and Minos too.
sentences.i: Jupiter's words moved the gods, and none of them can bring himself to go on complaining, seeing Rhadamanthus and Aeacus, and Minos, worn out by their years.
sentences.n: movere is not the infinitive of moveo but movērunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre; you will meet the form twice more in this part, at habuere and timuere. sustinet stands near the end of line 439 and the infinitive that completes it, queri, does not arrive until line 441. cum videat is causal cum with the subjunctive; fessos ... annis is an ablative of cause, worn out by the years.

sentences.t:
Qui, dum fuit integer aevi,
terruerat magnas ipso quoque nomine gentes.
sentences.l:
And he, while he was still unbroken in his prime,
had terrified great nations by his very name too.
sentences.i: And Minos, while his strength was still whole, had terrified great nations by his very name too.
sentences.n: Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative — “and he”, that is Minos — a thing Latin does constantly and English will not do, so the pronoun has to become a demonstrative. integer aevi is a genitive of respect, “sound in point of age”. terruerat is pluperfect and pushes that terror back behind the story's own past. ipso quoque nomine is quoque the adverb again, “by his very name too”.

sentences.t:
Tunc erat invalidus Deionidenque iuventae
robore Miletum Phoeboque parente superbum
pertimuit credensque suis insurgere regnis,
haud tamen est patriis arcere penatibus ausus.
sentences.l:
Then he was without strength, and Miletus, Deione's son,
proud with the vigour of youth and with Phoebus for a father,
he dreaded — and, believing him to be rising against his own realm,
he did not for all that dare to bar him from his ancestral household gods.
sentences.i: By then his strength was gone, and he came to dread Miletus, Deione's son, proud in the vigour of his youth and in having Phoebus for a father; and though he believed the man was rising against his kingdom, he still did not dare to shut him out of his ancestral home.
sentences.n: Deioniden keeps its Greek ending in the accusative, “son of Deione”, with Miletum standing in apposition to it. iuventae robore and Phoeboque parente are both ablatives of cause explaining superbum. credens governs an indirect statement whose accusative subject, eum, is simply left out. arcere takes an ablative of separation, patriis penatibus; the Penates are the household gods, and stand for home itself. patrius here is “ancestral, of one's native place”, not “belonging to his father” — the father just named is Phoebus, and these are the gods of the house Miletus grew up in. ausus est is semi-deponent — passive in form, active in meaning.

sentences.t:
Sponte fugis, Milete, tua, celerique carina
Aegaeas metiris aquas et in Aside terra
moenia constituis positoris habentia nomen.
sentences.l:
Of your own will you flee, Miletus, and with a swift keel
you measure out the Aegean waters, and in the land of Asia
you found walls that bear the name of their founder.
sentences.i: You flee of your own accord, Miletus; you measure out the Aegean in a swift ship, and in Asia you found a city that carries its founder's name.
sentences.n: Ovid turns from telling the story to addressing Miletus directly — an apostrophe, and the verbs go into the second person and the present tense. sponte ... tua is split around the vocative Milete, so the address falls inside the phrase. metiris is deponent, passive in form and active in meaning: “you measure out”. Aside is the Greek form of the adjective for Asia. positoris habentia nomen names the city without naming it: it is Miletus, called after the man.

sentences.t:
Hic tibi, dum sequitur patriae curvamina ripae,
filia Maeandri totiens redeuntis eodem
cognita Cyanee, praestantia corpora forma,
Byblida cum Cauno, prolem est enixa gemellam.
sentences.l:
There, while she was following the windings of her father's bank,
Cyanee — daughter of Maeander, the river so often returning to the same place —
known by you, surpassing as to her body in beauty,
brought forth Byblis together with Caunus, twin offspring.
sentences.i: There, while she followed the bends of her father's bank, Cyanee — daughter of Maeander, the river that keeps doubling back on itself — whom you had known, and whose body surpassed all others in beauty, bore Byblis and Caunus at a single birth, a pair of twins.
sentences.n: cognita, from cognosco, has tibi as its dative of agent: “known by you”. That is the ordinary decorous Latin for sleeping with someone, and the English keeps the same decorum the Latin has. Maeander is the winding river of Asia Minor whose name English still uses; totiens redeuntis eodem describes the bends. Magnus prints praestantia, neuter plural agreeing with corpora, so corpora is an accusative of respect — “surpassing as to her body, in beauty”; some editions print praestanti instead, making forma an ablative of description. est enixa is from the deponent enitor, passive in form and active in meaning: she is the one who bore them. Byblida keeps its Greek ending in the accusative.

sentences.t: Byblis in exemplo est, ut ament concessa puellae:
sentences.l: Byblis stands as the example, that girls should love what is permitted:
sentences.i: Byblis is there as the warning: that girls should love only what is allowed.
sentences.n: in exemplo est is the idiom for standing as an example, and here it is a cautionary one. concessa is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, “the things granted”. ut ament gives the purpose the example serves. The moral arrives before the story does: the reader is told the verdict, and only then what happened.

sentences.t:
Byblis Apollinei correpta cupidine fratris:
non soror ut fratrem, nec qua debebat, amabat.
sentences.l:
Byblis, seized by desire for her Apolline brother:
she did not love him as a sister a brother, nor in the way she ought.
sentences.i: Byblis was seized by desire for her brother, Apollo's descendant: she loved him, but not as a sister loves a brother, and not in the way she ought to have.
sentences.n: Line 455 has no finite verb of its own — correpta is left standing as a participle, and the colon hands the sentence over to amabat in the next line. Apollinei looks back to Miletus, son of Phoebus, so Caunus is Apollo's grandson. The double negative measures a proper love twice, by kind (non soror ut fratrem) and by manner (nec qua debebat), and denies both; debebat is imperfect, so the obligation stood the whole time.

sentences.t:
Illa quidem primo nullos intellegit ignes
nec peccare putat, quod saepius oscula iungat,
quod sua fraterno circumdet bracchia collo,
mendacique diu pietatis fallitur umbra.
sentences.l:
She indeed at first makes out no fires,
and does not think she does wrong because she joins kisses rather often,
because she puts her own arms about her brother's neck,
and for a long while she is deceived by the lying shadow of family love.
sentences.i: At first she does not recognise the fire at all, and sees no wrong in kissing him rather often, in putting her arms round her brother's neck; and for a long time the false shadow of sisterly duty deceives her.
sentences.n: ignes, “fires”, is the standing Latin metaphor for love, and Byblis will keep returning to it. The two quod clauses take the subjunctive, iungat and circumdet, because they give the reason as she puts it to herself, not as the poem asserts it. fallitur is passive: she is the one deceived. pietas is the dutiful affection owed to family, and umbra makes it a shadow that only resembles the real thing.

sentences.t:
Paulatim declinat amor, visuraque fratrem
culta venit nimiumque cupit formosa videri
et siqua est illic formosior, invidet illi.
sentences.l:
Little by little the love swerves aside, and, about to see her brother,
she comes dressed with care and wants too much to seem beautiful,
and if any woman there is more beautiful, she envies her.
sentences.i: Little by little her love goes off course; she comes to see her brother carefully dressed, and wants far too much to look beautiful — and if there is a lovelier girl there, she is jealous of her.
sentences.n: declinat is intransitive here: the love itself swerves from its course. visura is a future participle, “meaning to see”, giving the purpose of her coming. culta is the word for a woman groomed and dressed with art. invidet takes the dative, illi. Nothing in the line is stated as a change of mind — it is all conduct, watched from outside.

sentences.t:
Sed nondum manifesta sibi est nullumque sub illo
igne facit votum: verumtamen aestuat intus.
sentences.l:
But she is not yet plain to herself, and under that fire
she makes no vow: and yet, all the same, she seethes within.
sentences.i: But she is not yet clear to herself, and makes no prayer under that fire — and yet, all the same, she burns inside.
sentences.n: manifesta sibi est says it the Latin way round: she is the thing not yet visible, not the one failing to see. votum facere is the ordinary phrase for making a vow or prayer to a god, so what she has not yet done is ask for anything. verumtamen is a heavy double adversative, “but nevertheless”, and it is where the sentence turns.

sentences.t: Iam dominum appellat, iam nomina sanguinis odit:
sentences.l: Now she calls him master, now she hates the names of blood:
sentences.i: Now she is calling him her master; now she hates the words of kinship:
sentences.n: dominus is the title a lover gives the beloved in Latin love poetry, where the lover plays the slave. By using it she moves him out of the family and into the roles of elegy. nomina sanguinis are the kinship words themselves — brother, sister — and it is the words she hates first. The repeated iam ... iam sets the two motions side by side as one.

sentences.t: Byblida iam mavult, quam se vocet ille sororem.
sentences.l: She now prefers that he call her Byblis rather than sister.
sentences.i: She would rather he called her Byblis than sister.
sentences.n: mavult takes a bare subjunctive clause with no ut — vocet — a common economy in verse; quam ... sororem completes the comparison. The one verb expressed, vocet, has se for its object and sororem for its predicate; Byblida is the predicate of that same verb understood in the first half, which is why it stands outside the quam clause. Byblida keeps its Greek ending in the accusative.

sentences.i: Waking, though, she did not dare let those foul hopes sink into her own mind; but slackened by gentle sleep, she often sees the thing she loves;
sentences.n: obscenus is a hard word — foul, and also ill-omened — and it is here the poem's word for her hopes; at line 509 she will use it herself, of her own flames. demittere in animum is the idiom for letting a thought sink in and be entertained; here animo is a bare dative of direction where prose would write in animum. ausa est is semi-deponent, passive in form and active in meaning. vigilans marks the division the whole passage turns on: what she refuses awake, sleep hands her.

sentences.t:
visa est quoque iungere fratri
corpus et erubuit, quamvis sopita iacebat.
sentences.l:
She seemed, too, to join her body to her brother,
and she blushed, although she was lying deep asleep.
sentences.i: In the dream she was joining her body to her brother's, too; and she blushed for it, though she lay fast asleep.
sentences.n: visa est is videor with the infinitive, “she seemed” — the regular way of saying what a dream showed, so this is what she dreamt she did. quoque is the adverb again, “also”. quamvis governs the indicative iacebat rather than the subjunctive it usually takes, a licence of verse. The blush is the point of the couplet: the body answers before she is awake to give it leave.

sentences.t:
Somnus abit: silet illa diu repetitque quietis
ipsa suae speciem dubiaque ita mente profatur:
sentences.l:
Sleep goes: she is silent a long while and goes back over,
herself, the vision of her own rest, and thus, with a wavering mind, she speaks out:
sentences.i: Sleep goes. She lies silent a long while, going back over the vision her own sleep had given her, and then, with a mind divided, she speaks out:
sentences.n: species is the shape or vision a dream presents. ipsa is emphatic: the going back over it is her own doing, deliberate and unprompted. profatur is deponent, passive in form and active in meaning, and it is a solemn verb, the one used to announce a formal speech — which is what follows.

sentences.t:
“Me miseram! tacitae quid vult sibi noctis imago?
Quam nolim rata sit! cur haec ego somnia vidi?
sentences.l:
“Wretched me! What does the image of the silent night want for itself?
How I would not have it ratified! Why have I seen these dreams?
sentences.i: “Oh, wretched me! What does this vision of the silent night mean? How I wish it might never come true! Why have I seen such dreams?
sentences.n: me miseram is an accusative of exclamation, standing alone without a verb. quid sibi vult, literally “what does it want for itself”, is the ordinary Latin for “what does it mean?”. ratus, from reor, is the word for a thing confirmed and made binding, used of prayers granted and of dreams that come true; nolim is a potential subjunctive, “I should not wish”. She opens by disowning the dream, and the rest of the speech takes that back by degrees.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem est oculis quamvis formosus iniquis
et placet, et possim, si non sit frater, amare,
et me dignus erat. Verum nocet esse sororem.—
sentences.l:
He indeed is beautiful, however unfriendly the eyes,
and he pleases me, and I could love him, if he were not my brother,
and he was worthy of me. But it does harm to be a sister.—
sentences.i: He is handsome, though — handsome to the most grudging eyes — and he pleases me, and I could love him, if he were not my brother; and he was worthy of me. But it is being a sister that does the harm.—
sentences.n: quamvis ... iniquis is concessive, “however grudging the eyes may be”: she is arguing that his beauty is not her partiality. possim and sit are potential and ideal subjunctives, “I could love him, were he not my brother”. dignus takes the ablative, me. nocet is impersonal — “it does harm” — with the accusative and infinitive esse sororem and its subject me left out, so the harm is stated as a fact and nobody is named as harmed.

sentences.t:
Dummodo tale nihil vigilans committere temptem,
saepe licet simili redeat sub imagine somnus!
testis abest somno, nec abest imitata voluptas.
sentences.l:
Provided that, waking, I attempt to commit nothing of the kind,
let sleep come back often under a like image!
A witness is absent from sleep, and the pleasure that copies it is not absent.
sentences.i: So long as I attempt nothing of the kind while awake — let sleep come back often, and in the same shape! There is no witness to a dream, and the pleasure it counterfeits is there all the same.
sentences.n: dummodo with the subjunctive temptem sets a proviso, “provided only that”. licet here is the verb, “it is permitted”, with redeat as its subjunctive, not the concessive “although”: she is granting sleep a licence. imitata is from the deponent imitor, so it is active in meaning — the pleasure that imitates, not a pleasure imitated. The couplet is a piece of moral book-keeping: nothing done, nobody watching, and the pleasure kept.

sentences.t:
Pro! Venus et tenera volucer cum matre Cupido,
gaudia quanta tuli! quam me manifesta libido
contigit! ut iacui totis resoluta medullis!
sentences.l:
Ah! Venus, and winged Cupid with your tender mother —
what joys I carried away! how unmistakable the lust
that touched me! how I lay, loosened through all my marrow!
sentences.i: Ah — Venus, and winged Cupid at your tender mother's side — what joys I had of it! How plain the lust was that reached me! How I lay, undone to the very marrow!
sentences.n: pro is an interjection of appeal, used in calling on gods by name. Cupid is invoked together with his mother, who has just been named on her own account — the doubling belongs to the high style of the address. libido is the blunt Latin word for sexual desire and is left blunt here. medullae, the marrow, is where Latin poetry puts the seat of passion, so totis resoluta medullis says the whole body gave way. Three exclamations run one to a clause, each with its own exclamatory word: quanta, quam, ut.

sentences.t:
ut meminisse iuvat! quamvis brevis illa voluptas
noxque fuit praeceps et coeptis invida nostris.
sentences.l:
How it delights to remember! though that pleasure was brief,
and the night was headlong and grudging towards our beginnings.
sentences.i: How sweet it is to remember! — though the pleasure was short, and the night ran away headlong, jealous of what we had begun.
sentences.n: iuvat is impersonal, “it pleases”, with meminisse for its subject; meminisse is a perfect infinitive with present force, since the verb has no present. quamvis again takes the indicative, fuit. invida governs the dative coeptis nostris. nostris is the plural she uses of herself — though in a dream of the two of them it can be heard as “ours”, and the Latin does not decide.

sentences.t:
O ego, si liceat mutato nomine iungi,
quam bene, Caune, tuo poteram nurus esse parenti!
quam bene, Caune, meo poteras gener esse parenti!
sentences.l:
O — if only it were allowed me to be joined with the name changed —
how well, Caunus, I could have been a daughter-in-law to your father!
how well, Caunus, you could have been a son-in-law to mine!
sentences.i: Oh, if only I might be joined to him under a changed name — how well, Caunus, I could have been your father's daughter-in-law! how well, Caunus, you could have been my father's son-in-law!
sentences.n: mutato nomine is an ablative absolute: “with the name changed”. The name is “sister”, and what she wants altered is the relation, not the person. iungi is the passive infinitive used of marriage, “to be joined”. The two lines answer each other word for word with only the roles swapped, nurus for gener and tuo parenti for meo parenti, and the repeated quam bene, Caune holds the pairing exact. poteram and poteras are imperfect indicatives where English wants “could have been”: Latin regularly leaves an unreal possibility with posse in the indicative.

sentences.t:
Omnia, di facerent, essent communia nobis,
praeter avos: tu me vellem generosior esses!
sentences.l:
All things — would the gods might grant it — would be shared between us,
except our forebears: I could wish you were higher-born than I!
sentences.i: Let everything be ours in common — the gods grant it! — everything but our ancestors: I could wish you were of nobler blood than I am!
sentences.n: di facerent is a parenthetical optative subjunctive, “would that the gods might do it”, dropped inside its own sentence; vellem in the next line does the same work. avos, strictly grandfathers, stands for the whole line of ancestors — the one thing she wants not held in common. me is an ablative of comparison after generosior. The wish is exact: she would take the lower rank of the two, if that bought them different blood.

sentences.t: Nescioquam facies igitur, pulcherrime, matrem:
sentences.l: Some woman or other, then, you will make a mother, most beautiful one:
sentences.i: So you will make a mother of some woman I do not know, my beautiful one:
sentences.n: Nescioquam is nescio quis written as one word, the indefinite “some ... I know not whom”. facies is the future of facio with a double accusative, “you will make her a mother”. pulcherrime is vocative: she is addressing him, and he is not there. The colon sets up the answering clause about herself.

sentences.t:
at mihi, quae male sum quos tu sortita parentes,
nil nisi frater eris. Quod obest, id habebimus unum.
sentences.l:
but to me, who to my sorrow have drawn the very parents you drew,
you will be nothing but a brother. What stands in the way — that is the one thing we shall have.
sentences.i: But to me, who to my cost drew the same parents you drew, you will be nothing but a brother. The one thing we shall share is the thing that blocks us.
sentences.n: sortita sum is from the deponent sortior — passive in form, active in meaning: “I have drawn by lot”, not “I was allotted”. male is adverbial, “to my misfortune”. The relative clause carries a second relative inside it, quos tu ... parentes, whose verb has to be supplied from sum sortita. obest, from obsum, is “to stand in the way”; unum is predicative — the single thing they will possess is the very obstacle.

sentences.t:
Quid mihi significant ergo mea visa?—quod autem
somnia pondus habent?—
sentences.l:
What, then, do my own visions signify to me? — and anyway,
what weight do dreams carry? —
sentences.i: What are my visions telling me, then? — and in any case, what weight do dreams carry? —
sentences.n: visa, “things seen”, is the ordinary noun for what appears in a dream. quod is the interrogative adjective with pondus, “what weight”. The dashes are the edition's, and they mark the joints of the argument: she puts a question, then answers it with another, and will reverse again in the next line.

sentences.t: an habent et somnia pondus?
sentences.l: or do dreams have weight too?
sentences.i: Or perhaps dreams do carry weight after all?
sentences.n: an turns the previous question round: she has just implied dreams carry none, and an offers the opposite. et here is “also, even”, not “and”. The movement runs from line 495 to line 496 and reverses twice on the way — the shape of the whole speech in miniature.

sentences.t: Di melius!—di nempe suas habuere sorores:
sentences.l: May the gods do better than that! — the gods, to be sure, have had sisters of their own:
sentences.i: Heaven forbid! — and yet the gods, sure enough, have had sisters for wives:
sentences.n: di melius is an ellipse — a verb such as faciant is left out — and it is the standing Latin for “heaven forbid”. habuere is habuērunt, the -ēre perfect again. nempe carries a shrug, “why, of course”. She refuses the thought and, inside the same line, produces the precedent that undoes the refusal.

sentences.t:
Sic Saturnus Opem iunctam sibi sanguine duxit,
Oceanus Tethyn, Iunonem rector Olympi.
sentences.l:
So Saturn took to wife Ops, joined to him by blood;
Oceanus took Tethys; the ruler of Olympus took Juno.
sentences.i: So Saturn married Ops, his own blood; Oceanus married Tethys; and the ruler of Olympus married Juno.
sentences.n: duxit is short for uxorem duxit, “led home as a wife”, the standard Latin for a man marrying; it has to be supplied twice more, for Oceanus and for Jupiter. Tethyn keeps its Greek ending in the accusative. rector Olympi is Jupiter, named by his office rather than by name; he and Juno are brother and sister, which is the point of the list and the reason it ends with him.

sentences.t: Sunt superis sua iura!
sentences.l: There are, for the gods above, laws of their own!
sentences.i: The gods above have laws of their own!
sentences.n: sunt superis sua iura is a dative of possession — literally “there are to the gods their own laws” — which is how Latin most often says that someone has something. In four words she takes back the precedent she has just built out of Saturn, Oceanus and Jupiter: those laws hold for gods, and she is not one.

sentences.t:
Quid ad caelestia ritus
exigere humanos diversaque foedera tempto?
sentences.l:
Why do I try to measure human usages against the things of heaven,
and compacts that are nothing like them?
sentences.i: Why am I trying to hold human custom up against the standard of heaven, when the two sets of rules are nothing alike?
sentences.n: exigere ad is the idiom for testing a thing against a measure — the image is a builder's rule laid along the work. ritus and foedera are both accusative objects of exigere, split around it, and caelestia is neuter plural, “the things of heaven”. She has caught herself arguing out of the wrong law-book, and says so.

sentences.t:
Aut nostro vetitus de corde fugabitur ardor,
aut hoc si nequeo, peream, precor, ante toroque
mortua conponar, positaeque det oscula frater.—
sentences.l:
Either the forbidden blaze will be driven out of my heart,
or, if I cannot do that, I pray I may die first, and be laid out
dead upon the couch, and that my brother give kisses to me as I lie there.—
sentences.i: Either the forbidden fire will be driven out of my heart, or, if I cannot manage that, then let me die first — I pray for it — and be laid out dead on the bier, and let my brother kiss me where I lie.—
sentences.n: fugabitur and conponar are passive: the fire is driven out, she is laid out, and she never makes herself the agent of either. conpono is the ordinary verb for laying a body out for burial, and torus is both the marriage-couch and the bier — which is the whole force of the wish. positae is a dative agreeing with an unexpressed mihi, “to me, laid out”. precor governs peream, conponar and det without any ut.

sentences.t: Et tamen arbitrium quaerit res ista duorum.
sentences.l: And yet that business calls for the decision of two.
sentences.i: And even so, that business needs two people to decide it.
sentences.n: iste is the demonstrative that points at a thing with distance or distaste in it, so res ista holds her own plan away from her. arbitrium is a formal word, an arbitrator's ruling. Having argued herself the whole way round, she arrives at the one thing no argument of hers can supply: his agreement.

sentences.t: Finge placere mihi: scelus esse videbitur illi!
sentences.l: Suppose it pleases me: it will seem a crime to him!
sentences.i: Suppose I could bring myself to it — to him it will look like a crime!
sentences.n: finge is the imperative of fingo, “shape, imagine”, addressed by Byblis to herself; placere is an indirect statement whose subject is left out. scelus is the strong word — not a fault but a crime, an outrage. videbitur illi puts the verdict in his mouth, and the future indicative states it as what will happen, not what might.

sentences.t: At non Aeolidae thalamos timuere sororum!
sentences.l: But the sons of Aeolus did not fear their sisters' bedchambers!
sentences.i: But the sons of Aeolus did not shrink from their sisters' beds!
sentences.n: timuere is timuērunt, the -ēre perfect, the third in this part. thalamus is the bedchamber and, by extension, the marriage. The children of Aeolus were the standing Greek example of brother-sister marriage, and she reaches for them in the very line after admitting he will call it a crime: the argument runs on precedent because it has nothing else left.

sentences.t: Unde sed hos novi? Cur haec exempla paravi?
sentences.l: But from where do I know of these? Why have I got these examples ready?
sentences.i: But how do I come to know of them? Why have I had these examples ready?
sentences.n: sed is postponed to second place in its clause, which verse does freely. novi is a perfect with present force, “I know”. paravi is the word that catches her: the examples were got ready in advance, so the case was prepared before she began pleading it — and she is the one who notices.

sentences.t: Quo feror? Obscenae procul hinc discedite flammae,
sentences.l: Where am I being carried? Foul flames, depart far from here,
sentences.i: Where am I being swept? Away with you, foul flames, far from here —
sentences.n: feror is passive: she makes herself the thing carried, not the one going. obscenae picks up obscenas at line 468, where it was the poem's word for her hopes; here it is her own word, for her own flames. discedite is a plural imperative addressed to the flames themselves, as if they were something outside her that could be sent away.

sentences.t: nec, nisi qua fas est germanae, frater ametur!—
sentences.l: and let my brother not be loved, except in the way that is right for a sister!—
sentences.i: and let my brother not be loved, except as a sister may rightly love him!—
sentences.n: ametur is a jussive subjunctive, and it is passive: “let him be loved”, not “let me love him”. Even in the renunciation she keeps herself out of the grammar. fas is what divine law allows, as against ius, what human law allows; qua is the relative ablative of manner, “in the way in which”, and germanae is the dative, “for a sister”.

sentences.t:
Si tamen ipse mei captus prior esset amore,
forsitan illius possem indulgere furori.
sentences.l:
If, though, he himself had first been taken by love of me,
perhaps I could give way to his madness.
sentences.i: If he had been the first to be caught by love of me, though — then perhaps I could give way to his madness.
sentences.n: mei is an objective genitive, “love directed at me”, not “my love”. captus esset is pluperfect subjunctive, so the case is unreal and set in the past: a world in which he had already spoken first. forsitan regularly takes the subjunctive, here possem. indulgere governs the dative furori, and furor is the word for the madness of love, which she allows for him at line 512, two lines after ordering her own flames off at line 510.

sentences.t:
Ergo ego, quae fueram non reiectura petentem,
ipsa petam! Poterisne loqui? poterisne fateri?
Coget amor: potero!
sentences.l:
So I, who would not have been the one to refuse him if he asked,
shall do the asking myself! Will you be able to speak? will you be able to confess?
Love will compel: I shall be able!
sentences.i: So I, who would not have refused him had he asked, am to be the one asking! Can you speak it? can you confess it? Love will force it — yes, I can!
sentences.n: reiectura with fueram is a periphrastic future participle that puts the whole unreal case in the past: “I who would not have been going to refuse”. petentem, “one asking”, is masculine and means him; ipsa petam takes the same verb and gives it to her. Then she turns and addresses herself in the second person, poterisne, twice over, and answers in the first, potero — the two halves of her arguing are given two grammatical persons.

sentences.t:
vel, si pudor ora tenebit,
littera celatos arcana fatebitur ignis:
sentences.l:
or, if shame holds my lips, a secret letter
will confess the fires I have hidden:
sentences.i: or, if shame stops my mouth, a secret letter will confess the fire I have kept hidden:
sentences.n: ignis here is the accusative plural, the older form of ignes, and it is the object of fatebitur, not a nominative singular — Magnus prints ignis and some editions print ignes. fatebitur is from the deponent fateor, passive in form and active in meaning: the letter does the confessing, and she does not. celatos is the participle, fires kept hidden. ora tenere is the idiom for shame stopping the mouth.

sentences.t: hoc placet, haec dubiam vicit sententia mentem.”
sentences.l: this pleases me; this decision has conquered my wavering mind.”
sentences.i: this is what I choose; this resolve has won my wavering mind over.”
sentences.n: sententia is a vote or a considered opinion, so the decision is presented as the winning side in a debate — which is exactly what the speech has been. vicit ... mentem makes the mind the thing defeated, not the thing choosing. The perfect closes the soliloquy: the arguing is over.

sentences.t:
In latus erigitur cubitoque innixa sinistro
“viderit: insanos” inquit “fateamur amores.
Ei mihi! quo labor? quem mens mea concipit ignem?”
sentences.l:
She raises herself onto her side, and, propped on her left elbow,
“let him see to it,” she says, “let us confess this mad love.
Ah me! where am I slipping? what fire is my mind taking in?”
sentences.i: She raises herself on her side, propped on her left elbow. “Let him see to it,” she says; “let us confess this mad love. Ah me — where am I sliding? what fire is my mind catching?”
sentences.n: viderit is a future perfect used as a set phrase, “let him see to it” — she hands the judgement over to him. innixa is from the deponent innitor, active in meaning, and takes the ablative cubito sinistro. fateamur is a hortatory subjunctive, and a plural she uses of herself alone. labor here is the deponent labi, “I slip”, not labor “I toil”: the two are spelled the same in this form. She settles the question at line 519 and comes apart again in the line after it.

sentences.t:
et meditata manu componit verba trementi:
dextra tenet ferrum, vacuam tenet altera ceram.
sentences.l:
and with a trembling hand she sets in order the words she has thought out:
her right hand holds the iron, the other holds the empty wax.
sentences.i: and with a trembling hand she arranges the words she has been rehearsing: her right hand holds the stylus, the other the blank wax.
sentences.n: meditata is from the deponent meditor and is active in meaning: words she has thought over, not words thought over by someone else. manu ... trementi is a single ablative phrase split around componit verba, so the trembling frames the composing. ferrum, “iron”, is the metal stylus; the cera is the wax-coated tablet, written on with the stylus's point and smoothed flat again with its blunt end — which is what the next lines describe.

sentences.t:
Incipit et dubitat, scribit damnatque tabellas
et notat et delet, mutat culpatque probatque,
sentences.l:
She begins and hesitates; she writes and condemns the tablets;
she marks and rubs out, she changes and blames and approves,
sentences.i: She begins and hesitates; she writes, and condemns what she has written; she marks the wax and rubs it out; she alters, faults it, passes it,
sentences.n: Nine finite verbs stand in these two lines, nearly all strung together with et and -que; the piling up of connectives is what makes the indecision audible. The pairs cancel each other as they go: writes and condemns, marks and erases, faults and approves. tabellae are the pair of hinged wax tablets a letter was written on.

sentences.t: inque vicem sumptas ponit positasque resumit.
sentences.l: and by turns she lays down what she has taken up and takes up again what she has laid down.
sentences.i: and by turns she puts down what she has picked up, and picks up again what she has put down.
sentences.n: sumptas and positas are perfect participles agreeing with tabellas, understood from line 523 two lines above. The line is built as a mirror — sumptas ponit, positas resumit — the same two verbs crossed over, with re- in resumit sending the whole motion round once more. The word order performs the wavering that the sense reports.

sentences.t:
Quid velit ignorat; quidquid factura videtur,
displicet. In vultu est audacia mixta pudori.
sentences.l:
She does not know what she wants; whatever she seems about to do
displeases her. In her face there is boldness mixed with shame.
sentences.i: She does not know what she wants; whatever she seems on the point of doing displeases her. In her face, boldness is mixed with shame.
sentences.n: quid velit is an indirect question and takes the subjunctive. factura videtur is a future participle with videor, “she seems about to do” — a seeming, which is what an onlooker would report, and the poem has been watching her from outside ever since her speech broke off at line 520. mixta takes the dative pudori, the regular construction for mixing one thing with another. The two halves of her are named at last, and named as one expression on a face.

sentences.t:
Scripta “soror” fuerat, visum est delere sororem
verbaque correctis incidere talia ceris:
sentences.l:
“Sister” had been written; it seemed best to erase the “sister”
and to cut such words as these into the corrected wax:
sentences.i: The word “sister” had been written; she decided to erase the “sister”, and to cut words like these into the smoothed-over wax:
sentences.n: scripta fuerat is a pluperfect passive built with fuerat rather than erat, an older and heavier form, and it names no writer: the word had been written, as though by nobody. sororem is the word itself, treated as a thing that can be deleted, and deleting it is the whole action of the passage. correctis ceris is wax smoothed flat with the blunt end of the stylus so that it can be written on again. visum est is impersonal, “it seemed good”. The colon opens onto the letter.
